blocks.content: A deploy kicks off. Somewhere in the fleet, an orchestrator decides an old instance of your service needs to go away and a new one should take its place. At that exact moment, that old instance might be halfway through writing an order to the database, holding a message pulled off a queue, or streaming a response to a waiting client.

What happens next decides whether that deploy is invisible to users or whether it quietly drops requests, corrupts partial writes, or loses a message nobody ever sees again. That difference is graceful shutdown: the discipline of stopping a running process in a way that finishes what it is doing before it actually stops.

It sounds like a small detail next to bigger architectural decisions, but it is one of the few things that separates a deploy users never notice from one that generates a burst of errors and a support queue full of confused reports.

It also compounds. A service that deploys once a week can get away with a sloppy shutdown for a long time before anyone notices the pattern. A service that deploys dozens of times a day, or autoscales constantly, hits this every single time, and the cost adds up fast.

This topic covers what actually happens when a process is asked to stop, why killing it abruptly is dangerous, the shutdown sequence a well behaved service follows, how it interacts with health checks, and how it all connects to deploying new code without downtime.

None of this requires exotic infrastructure. It is almost entirely a matter of writing a small amount of deliberate code in the right place and the right order, which is exactly why it is worth understanding thoroughly rather than copying a snippet without knowing why each step exists.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530480-750301540.png
blocks.alt: An orchestrator sends SIGTERM, the app drains its work, then exits cleanly

blocks.content: 1. What Happens When a Process Is Told to Stop
blocks.text: 1. What Happens When a Process Is Told to Stop

blocks.content: In a modern deployment, processes are stopped constantly and on purpose. An orchestrator like Kubernetes scales a service down when load drops, rolls instances during a deploy, or replaces an unhealthy pod. None of this is a crash, it is a deliberate, routine instruction: stop running.

The mechanism is almost always the same. The orchestrator sends the process a SIGTERM signal, a polite request to terminate, and gives it a window of time to shut itself down cleanly. Only if that window expires does it escalate to a forced kill.

What the process does inside that window is entirely up to the application. A process that ignores the signal, or has never been written to handle it, is functionally no different from one that is killed outright the moment the window runs out.

Different orchestration platforms use slightly different terminology, a pod termination in Kubernetes, an instance drain in a managed load balancer, a task stop in a container scheduler, but underneath almost all of them the same SIGTERM and grace period mechanism is doing the work.

blocks.title: SIGTERM is a request, not a demand
blocks.content: SIGTERM asks a process to stop. It does not stop it. The process has to catch the signal and actually run its own shutdown logic, or the request goes unanswered until the grace period expires.

This happens far more often than most engineers assume. Autoscaling scales instances down as traffic drops, rolling deploys replace every instance in a fleet, and a single bad node gets drained and replaced automatically. A production service is stopped and started routinely, not just on the rare occasions someone manually restarts it.
2. Why Abruptly Killing a Process Is Dangerous
blocks.text: 2. Why Abruptly Killing a Process Is Dangerous

blocks.content: It is tempting to assume stopping a process is instantaneous and harmless, it is just a program ending. In practice a running service almost always has work in progress at any given moment: a request being handled, a database transaction half written, a message pulled off a queue but not yet acknowledged.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785286610963-224416223.png
blocks.alt: A forced kill drops in flight requests and can lose messages that were never fully processed

blocks.content: Kill the process outright, with a SIGKILL or the equivalent of unplugging it, and none of that in progress work gets a chance to finish. A client mid request gets a broken connection instead of a response. A transaction that was partway through several writes can leave the database in an inconsistent state if it is not wrapped safely. A queue message that was read but not acknowledged either gets silently lost or, depending on the broker, redelivered in a way the application never expected.

None of these are exotic edge cases, they are the routine cost of pretending shutdown is instantaneous when it never is. A service that is stopped and restarted dozens of times a day, which is normal in a container orchestrated environment, will hit this constantly if it is not handled.
The user-visible symptom

From the outside, none of this looks like a shutdown problem. It shows up as a small, recurring spike of five hundred errors or timed out requests that seems to correlate suspiciously well with deploy times, and gets dismissed as noise until someone actually connects the two.
Every deploy is a small, controlled outage unless the process being replaced is given a real chance to finish what it was doing first.
3. SIGTERM and SIGKILL

Two signals matter most here, and the difference between them is the whole reason graceful shutdown is possible at all. SIGTERM is catchable, the process can register a handler for it and run its own cleanup logic before exiting on its own terms. SIGKILL is not catchable by design, the operating system terminates the process immediately with no opportunity to run any code at all.

This is why the shutdown sequence lives entirely inside the SIGTERM handler. By the time SIGKILL arrives, if it ever does, there is nothing left to do, the process disappears mid instruction with no cleanup possible. Everything a service can do to shut down well has to happen in the window between those two signals.

A related signal worth knowing is SIGINT, sent when someone presses control-C in a terminal. It is catchable in the same way as SIGTERM, and most services handle both with the same shutdown logic, since a developer stopping a local process and an orchestrator stopping a deployed one deserve the same clean behavior.
4. The Graceful Shutdown Sequence

A well behaved service follows roughly the same sequence regardless of language or framework, and the order matters as much as the individual steps. Stopping in the wrong order can drop exactly the requests graceful shutdown is meant to save.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530480-95946614.png
blocks.alt: Stop accepting new work, drain what is in flight, close connections cleanly, then exit

blocks.content: ["Stop accepting new connections or requests, so nothing new starts arriving","Let requests already in progress finish naturally, this is the drain","Close database, queue, and cache connections only once nothing is using them","Exit the process cleanly, signaling success back to the orchestrator"]
items: Stop accepting new connections or requests, so nothing new starts arriving
Let requests already in progress finish naturally, this is the drain
Close database, queue, and cache connections only once nothing is using them
Exit the process cleanly, signaling success back to the orchestrator

blocks.content: Notice that closing connections comes after draining, not before. Closing a database connection while a request is still mid query does not save anything, it just turns a request that would have succeeded into one that fails with a connection error instead.

It is worth writing this sequence down explicitly rather than trusting it to be obvious, because the order is exactly what tends to get scrambled under the pressure of adding shutdown handling as an afterthought late in a project.
5. Draining In-Flight Requests

Draining is the heart of the whole sequence: once the server stops accepting new connections, it waits for the requests it already accepted to finish, rather than cutting them off. Most HTTP server libraries expose exactly this as a close method that stops listening for new connections while letting existing ones complete.

For a typical web request this takes milliseconds to a few seconds. For something longer, a file upload, a long running query, a streaming response, the drain has to genuinely wait rather than assume everything finishes instantly, which is exactly why a shutdown timeout, covered shortly, exists as a safety net rather than an afterthought.

A background worker draining a queue follows the same idea in a different shape: stop pulling new messages, finish processing whatever message is currently in hand, acknowledge it, and only then stop.
Long-lived connections need special care

A WebSocket or a long streaming response does not finish on its own the way a normal request does. Draining these usually means sending the client a signal to reconnect elsewhere, or waiting up to a bounded maximum before forcing them closed, rather than assuming they will wrap up naturally within a short window.
6. Closing Database and Queue Connections Cleanly
blocks.text: 6. Closing Database and Queue Connections Cleanly

blocks.content: Once nothing is actively using them, connections should be closed deliberately rather than left for the operating system to tear down when the process disappears. A connection pool that is closed cleanly releases its resources back to the database immediately; one that vanishes with the process can leave stale connections lingering on the database side until they time out.

Message queue clients deserve the same care. A consumer that is mid message when it shuts down should finish that message, acknowledge or reject it explicitly, and only then disconnect. Disconnecting first, or exiting before acknowledging, is exactly how a message that was actually completed gets redelivered and processed twice, or how one that was never finished gets silently dropped depending on the broker's defaults.

This connects directly to idempotent message handling. Even a carefully built shutdown sequence cannot guarantee zero duplicate deliveries across every possible failure timing, which is exactly why consumers should already be built to handle a message arriving twice, rather than relying on shutdown discipline alone to prevent it.

blocks.title: Order these last, not first
blocks.content: Database and queue connections should be the very last thing a shutdown sequence closes, after every in-flight request or message that depends on them has already finished.

For a connection pool specifically, closing it cleanly usually means waiting for every checked out connection to be returned first, rather than forcing them shut while a query might still be running on one of them.
7. Health Checks and Readiness Probes During Shutdown
blocks.text: 7. Health Checks and Readiness Probes During Shutdown

blocks.content: A subtle race condition sits right at the start of shutdown. The moment a process begins terminating, it needs to stop receiving new traffic, but the load balancer or orchestrator routing traffic to it does not know that instantly, it finds out through health checks, and health checks run on an interval, not in real time.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530481-143025873.png
blocks.alt: Marking the pod not ready and letting the load balancer deregister it avoids dropped requests

blocks.content: If a service just stops accepting connections the instant SIGTERM arrives, without warning anything upstream, some in flight traffic that was already routed to it, or traffic sent in the brief window before the load balancer notices, gets connection errors instead of clean responses.

This race is easy to miss in testing, because a lightly loaded staging environment rarely surfaces it. It shows up specifically under real production traffic, right at deploy time, which is exactly the situation nobody wants a subtle timing bug appearing in.

The fix is to flip the readiness probe to failing as the very first step of shutdown, before draining begins, so the load balancer or orchestrator starts routing new traffic elsewhere immediately. The process then waits briefly for that deregistration to actually take effect before it stops accepting connections, closing the exact race window that would otherwise drop requests.

["SIGTERM arrives, the process immediately marks itself not ready","The load balancer notices on its next health check and stops sending new traffic","The process waits a short buffer, then stops accepting new connections","In-flight requests drain normally while the process is already marked not ready"]
items: SIGTERM arrives, the process immediately marks itself not ready
The load balancer notices on its next health check and stops sending new traffic
The process waits a short buffer, then stops accepting new connections
In-flight requests drain normally while the process is already marked not ready

blocks.content: That short buffer is easy to underestimate, but skipping it is one of the most common causes of a brief error spike right at the start of a deploy, even in a system where every other part of the shutdown sequence is written correctly.
8. Shutdown Timeouts and Forced Kill

Draining cannot wait forever. A single stuck request, a hung database query, a connection that never closes, would otherwise block shutdown indefinitely and stall a deploy or a scale down. Every orchestrator enforces a grace period, a fixed amount of time the process is given after SIGTERM before it is killed outright with SIGKILL regardless of what it is doing.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530481-783365244.png
blocks.alt: If draining finishes within the grace period the exit is clean, otherwise SIGKILL forces it

blocks.content: Kubernetes defaults this to thirty seconds, and it is configurable per workload. Choosing that number is a real tradeoff: too short and normal requests get cut off mid drain during ordinary deploys, too long and a genuinely stuck shutdown blocks the deploy pipeline and delays rollbacks longer than necessary.

Workloads are not uniform here either. A stateless API handling short requests can usually get away with a fairly short grace period, while a worker processing long running jobs or large file uploads legitimately needs a longer one, and setting both to the same default is a common source of avoidable dropped work.

A well built shutdown handler treats this timeout as a real deadline inside the application too, not just something the orchestrator enforces from outside. Racing the drain against an internal timer and forcing an exit if it runs long avoids depending entirely on SIGKILL as the only backstop.

The reason an internal timer is worth the extra code is control. Exiting on your own terms lets you log exactly what was still in flight when the deadline hit, which is far more useful for debugging than an unexplained SIGKILL with no application level trace of what was stuck.
9. Connecting to Zero-Downtime Deployments

Graceful shutdown is not just about a single instance stopping cleanly, it is the piece that makes a rolling update actually deliver zero downtime. A rolling update replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, and the whole promise rests on each old instance finishing its work properly before it disappears.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396530482-311237888.png
blocks.alt: A new pod becomes ready, traffic shifts to it, and only then does the old pod exit

blocks.content: The sequence an orchestrator follows during a rolling update depends on graceful shutdown at every step: start a new instance, wait for its readiness probe to pass, shift traffic toward it, then send SIGTERM to an old instance and let it drain before removing it entirely. Skip graceful shutdown and this becomes a rolling series of small outages instead of a seamless transition.

This is also why graceful shutdown and fast startup are usually discussed together. A deploy is only as smooth as its slowest link, and a service that takes thirty seconds to become ready holds up the same rollout that a slow, careless shutdown would.

A scale down event tells the same story without a deploy involved at all. Traffic drops overnight, the orchestrator removes a few instances to save cost, and the exact same shutdown sequence runs, invisibly, hundreds of times a week in a system that autoscales.
10. A Practical Shutdown Handler

Put together, a shutdown handler for a typical HTTP service tends to look like this: mark not ready, wait briefly for deregistration, stop accepting new connections, drain in-flight ones, close downstream connections, and race the whole thing against a timeout.

None of these individual pieces are complicated on their own. What makes graceful shutdown easy to get wrong is forgetting one of them, especially the readiness flip at the very start, which is invisible in normal operation and only shows up as a burst of dropped requests during a deploy.

It is worth testing this deliberately rather than trusting it works, sending a real SIGTERM to a running instance under load and confirming no requests are dropped is a cheap, high value check that most teams skip until an incident forces the question.
11. Designing This in an Interview
Name the signal: I explain that an orchestrator sends SIGTERM to ask a process to stop, and the application has to catch it and run its own cleanup, or it is no better than a forced kill.

Walk the sequence in order: stop accepting new work, drain what is in flight, close downstream connections last, exit. I call out that the order matters, closing connections early breaks the very requests draining is meant to save.
Flag the readiness race: I mention marking the health check not-ready as the first step, so the load balancer stops routing new traffic before the process itself stops accepting it.

Bring up the timeout: I note that draining is bounded by a grace period, and that a well built handler races its own internal timer against it rather than relying solely on the orchestrator's SIGKILL as a backstop.
Connect it to deploys: I tie it back to rolling updates, explaining that zero downtime deployment depends on every old instance shutting down gracefully while new instances become ready in parallel.
12. Common Questions

What if my process cannot finish draining in time? It gets forcibly killed by SIGKILL once the grace period expires, which is why the grace period should be set generously enough for realistic request durations, and why a stuck drain is worth investigating rather than just extending the timeout indefinitely.

Does graceful shutdown matter for a single server with no load balancer? Less, but it still matters. Even a single instance can be mid transaction or mid message when it restarts, and losing that work is exactly as costly whether or not there is a fleet around it.

Is closing the process with process.exit() enough on its own? No. Calling exit without first draining and closing connections is the same abrupt stop graceful shutdown exists to avoid, it just happens to be triggered by your own code instead of the operating system.

How is this different from a health check used for startup? A readiness probe is checked continuously, both to confirm a new instance is ready to receive traffic and to signal, during shutdown, that it should stop receiving it. The same mechanism serves both directions of the lifecycle.

What is the right grace period to set? Long enough to cover your slowest realistic request or job under normal load, plus a margin, but not so long that a genuinely stuck shutdown delays a rollback during an incident. Measure real request durations rather than guessing.
13. Key Takeaways

["SIGTERM is a request to stop that a process can catch and handle; SIGKILL is an unconditional, uncatchable kill.","Abruptly killing a process drops in-flight requests, can corrupt partial writes, and can lose queue messages.","The shutdown sequence is: stop new work, drain existing work, close connections, then exit, in that order.","Flip the readiness probe to not-ready first, so the load balancer stops routing traffic before the process stops accepting it.","A shutdown grace period bounds how long draining can take before SIGKILL forces an exit anyway.","Graceful shutdown is what makes rolling updates and zero-downtime deployments actually work in practice."]
items: SIGTERM is a request to stop that a process can catch and handle; SIGKILL is an unconditional, uncatchable kill.
Abruptly killing a process drops in-flight requests, can corrupt partial writes, and can lose queue messages.
The shutdown sequence is: stop new work, drain existing work, close connections, then exit, in that order.
Flip the readiness probe to not-ready first, so the load balancer stops routing traffic before the process stops accepting it.
A shutdown grace period bounds how long draining can take before SIGKILL forces an exit anyway.
Graceful shutdown is what makes rolling updates and zero-downtime deployments actually work in practice.

blocks.content: None of the individual steps in a graceful shutdown are hard to write. What makes it worth real attention is how quietly it fails when skipped, a service can run for months without anyone noticing it drops a handful of requests on every single deploy.
